video_title: Washington Is Suppressing Volatility To Keep The AI Boom Alive | Weekly Roundup
gist: Three Forward Guidance hosts argue that volatility management has migrated from the Fed to the Treasury: Bessant funded a yen intervention by selling euros from the ESF (not dollars or bonds), pushed FIMA-facility usage, and quietly flipped the quarterly refunding language from 'increases' to 'changes' in coupon auction sizes — all to keep the long end calm so the debt-funded AI capex boom can continue into the midterms. They split on what it means: Tyler sees state-directed capitalism making industrials, power/nuclear and hyperscaler credit the secular longs, while Quinn warns the band-aids mask deteriorating Mag 7 fundamentals and are storing up inflation and tinder. It is Tyler Neville's final roundup before joining Shotton Capital.

themes.theme: Volatility suppression migrates from Fed to Treasury

insights.claim: Realized volatility at the index surface is far lower than the stress building underneath it, and policy intervention to suppress that stress will intensify rather than fade over the three months into the midterms.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Expect every vol spike to be met with a policy answer; fading vol spikes and owning inflation protection has an official-sector tailwind until November.
insights.quote: So get ready because every time yields start rising, the move starts rising, dollar starts rising, they seem to have an answer for it.

insights.claim: Control of market volatility has structurally shifted from the Federal Reserve to the Treasury, with Bessant acting as a Plaza-Accord-scale volatility suppressor rather than a volatility speculator.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Macro traders should watch Treasury announcements and FX operations, not just FOMC, as the primary volatility-setting event risk.
insights.quote: I just think we're we crossed some Rubicon of volatility controlling where it moved from the Fed to the Treasury.

insights.claim: Bessant, Worsh and Trump are in near-constant contact and time interventions to precise technical breaking points — the yen defense and euro sale landed exactly where TLT skew signalled yields were about to break out and spill into credit spreads.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Options skew in long-duration proxies like TLT becomes a leading indicator of when the official sector will step in — a tradeable reaction function.
insights.quote: So they're literally watching the charts just like we are at the breaking point when skew kind of like goes nuts.

insights.claim: Worsh's hawkish public posture is cosmetic cover: the Fed chair and Trump are reportedly speaking far more often than Trump and Powell ever did, which points to fiscal dominance rather than restored Fed independence.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Positioning built on a hawkish-Warsh normalization narrative (short gold, long real rates) is offside; gold's rally is already sniffing the pivot.
insights.quote: I think Warf and Trump have already talked way more than Trump and Powell ever did through probably both of his terms.

insights.claim: The Worsh Fed is simultaneously more free-market on the long end (letting the curve steepen) and more interventionist on the front end (skewing issuance to bills), and the net package — weaker dollar, repoing treasuries for liquidity, shorter coupon duration — is unambiguously stimulative and inflationary.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: The policy mix argues for curve steepeners, a lower dollar and higher breakevens even while headline rhetoric sounds hawkish.

insights.claim: Inflation running at three and a half percent with problematic oil, drained global reserves and sticky core means the stimulative interventions risk locking in a permanently higher inflation run rate, with the next supply shock capable of pushing it to five, six or seven percent.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: The distribution of inflation outcomes is skewed right; cheap upside inflation optionality and commodity exposure are asymmetric hedges.
insights.quote: Inflation is still three and a half%. Oil is problematic. Global reserves are drained. Like core is still very very high.

insights.claim: Suppressing every volatility event prevents the cleansing forest fire and accumulates tinder, so the medium-term health of markets is deteriorating even as the tape makes new highs.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Treat the intervention regime as raising tail risk rather than removing it; the payoff profile favors carry now, convexity later.
insights.quote: by not letting the the brush on the ground burn, you're accumulating tinder.

insights.claim: Despite the AI-related deleveraging episode, SPY, the Q's, IWM and RSP are all making or near new highs with market breadth improving, making the bull market hard to fade and single-stock vol spikes a long-term buying opportunity if stop losses are used.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Broadening breadth plus policy support argues for buying beaten-up AI-adjacent sectors on vol spikes rather than shorting the index.
insights.quote: you're seeing like the whole market breath is actually getting healthier right now even in the face of all this.

themes.theme: Treasury plumbing: ESF, FIMA and the QRA language flip

insights.claim: The yen intervention was funded by selling euros from the Exchange Stabilization Fund rather than selling dollars or liquidating bonds, deliberately avoiding any supply pressure on the long end of the Treasury curve.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: It is a template: future FX intervention can be run without bond supply, so don't expect yen defense to translate into Treasury selling.
insights.quote: he did not sell dollars uh to fund that. He sold euros from the ESF, the exchange stabilization fund.

insights.claim: Bessant is publicly encouraging usage of the Fed's FIMA repo facility — a Treasury Secretary promoting a Fed liquidity facility that functions much like the BTFP or swap lines, letting foreign officials borrow dollars against bonds instead of selling them.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: FIMA usage becomes a real-time gauge of covert dollar liquidity provision; rising drawdowns are a liquidity-positive signal for risk assets.

insights.claim: Because the dollar index is so heavily yen-weighted, the intervention delivered a lower DXY without any direct dollar selling — an effective weak-dollar policy executed without spooking the bond market.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A stealth weak-dollar regime supports dollar-liquidity-sensitive assets (gold, EM, commodities) without the usual rates backlash.
insights.quote: it feels to me like a way to get weaker dollar policy without spooking the bond market.

insights.claim: Now that hyperscaler operating cash flow is tapped out, the AI buildout is being financed in the debt markets, which are priced off the long end — making long-end stability a direct policy dependency of the AI capex cycle.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Long-bond yields are now the transmission channel to AI capex; a disorderly long end is the single clearest kill-switch for the AI trade.

insights.claim: The real target of the intervention is the global life insurance business model, which is structurally short volatility through asset-liability matching — FX and fixed income volatility forces those insurers to sell the bonds backing their liabilities, so policymakers want that model to degrade slowly rather than crack.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Japanese lifer hedging flows are the plumbing to watch; cross-currency basis and JGB/UST spreads signal when the backstop is being tested.
insights.quote: they're backstopping the the global life insurance business model which is essentially short volatility

insights.claim: The quarterly refunding announcement changed its standing language from evaluating potential future 'increases' to 'changes' in nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes, opening the door to coupon issuance cuts that were not on anyone's radar.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A dovish supply surprise for the long end — bullish duration and steepener-unwind risk; watch the next refunding for confirmation of actual cuts.
insights.quote: suddenly they're talking about changes which opens up the tale of decreases to coupon issuance which is I don't think that was on anybody's radar.

insights.claim: The 'increase' language had been in place for three or four consecutive quarters while issuance levels and TGA minimums kept growing, so the reversal is a large signal — and the strong demand being cited to justify less duration is coming from the Fed, effectively the government's other pocket.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Treat headline 'strong demand' for Treasuries skeptically when the marginal buyer is the central bank; it flatters the funding picture without private absorption.
insights.quote: the dem demand that's so great is coming from the Fed which is our other pocket.

insights.claim: Shifting funding from long duration to short is highly stimulative because it propels the wealth effect, which drives more than 50 percent of consumer spending, but it also degrades the price signals and braking mechanisms of the capital markets.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Bills-heavy funding is a de facto easing lever; it supports risk assets near term while making traditional market signals less reliable for timing.

themes.theme: State capitalism and the boomer-Ponzi deleveraging plan

insights.claim: The macro regime has shifted from twenty years of Fed-driven liquidity with weak fiscal — which widened the gap between balance-sheet owners and everyone else — to top-down geopolitical statecraft that directs growth toward chosen sectors, China-style, as the CHIPS Act did for semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Sector selection now follows policy direction rather than the discount rate; front-run announced national-priority sectors instead of trading the Fed.
insights.quote: It's it's statecraft. It's not just watch the Fed, you know,

insights.claim: Hyperscaler capex as a share of GDP is now higher than telecom capex as a share of GDP during the late-1990s/2000s boom, and it completely dwarfs that prior cycle on the same measure.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: The AI capex cycle is larger relative to the economy than the telecom bubble, which raises both the growth contribution and the downside if it stalls.
insights.quote: So hyperscaler capex as a share of GDP is higher than the telecom capex share of GDP in the 2000s.

insights.claim: Residential investment's historic share of GDP was largely a generational extraction mechanism that turned the next cohort into renters rather than rentiers, whereas hyperscaler capex could either replicate that with an AI oligarch class taxing users or actually be productive capital allocation that multiplies economic growth.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: The key question for the decade is whether AI capex earns a return or becomes a rent — it determines whether to own the toll-takers or the users.

insights.claim: The explicit policy path out of the debt problem is keeping financing costs below the inflation rate while growth holds up, which naturally delevers the economy over ten to twenty years by taxing bondholding boomers with inflation while new generations invest in growth.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Financial repression is the base case — own real assets and equities over nominal bonds unless real yields stay clearly positive.
insights.quote: that's how you work your way out of the boomer Ponzi scheme is boomers essentially take the the tax of inflation on all the bonds they own and the the the new generations invest in in growth.

insights.claim: Unlike 2008, when Lehman was intentionally allowed to fail and Congress delayed TARP until the last second, authorities now intervene at the first sign of bond market volatility and will throw everything at the AI buildout before conditions even get hairy.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: The reaction function is far earlier than in prior crises, which compresses drawdowns but raises the eventual moral-hazard bill.
insights.quote: this time at the first second of of bond market volatility, they're stifling it down.

insights.claim: Oracle bonds around eight to nine percent are a steal for an investment-grade company, and boomers would be better off selling equity to buy that credit for real yield.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: The actionable AI trade may be the debt, not the stock — IG hyperscaler paper at high single-digit yields with limited default risk.
insights.quote: you get oracle bonds at like say 8 9% %. That's a steal, man. This company, that's a investment grade company at eight or nine%, right?

insights.claim: Oracle CDS around 200 basis points versus CoreWeave's roughly 800 at the peak shows AI credit is not one asset class — the capital structures are entirely different and should not be traded as a bloc.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Dispersion trade: long IG hyperscaler credit against the levered, high-yield AI infrastructure names rather than a directional AI credit view.
insights.quote: it's like 200 some basis points whereas like I think core weaves was like 800 at the peak.

insights.claim: The Mag 7 have no buybacks left, negative cash flows and widening credit spreads, and none of the AI trade's fundamental cracks were repaired by the interventions — it is slow deterioration rather than crash risk.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Underweight the mega-cap AI leaders on a multi-week to multi-month view even if the index holds; the bid is policy, not fundamentals.
insights.quote: there's no buybacks left for the Meg 7. Their cash flows are negative. Their credit spreads are widening

insights.claim: Semiconductors and the Japan, Taiwan and Korea tech complex do not look good here even after the leverage washout, because the reversion has simply put them back in the prior trend without fixing anything.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Avoid or fade Asian tech and semis on bounces; the deleveraging cleared positioning but not the underlying fundamental problem.

insights.claim: State-directed investment into nuclear could produce an unprecedented energy surplus, with late-stage Series C and D rounds already flowing to fission, fusion and SMR companies such as Valor Atomics and ALO Atomics, partly to reduce strategic exposure to Hormuz oil.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: A commodity-abundance scenario is the main counterweight to the inflation thesis; nuclear and SMR exposure is the way to be long that outcome.
insights.quote: I think we're on the cusp of like a energy surplus that we've never seen before basically because they're going to state direct like right into nuclear power.

insights.claim: Because capital itself has been commoditized, power is the scarce backbone of a 21st-century economy and the place investors should be concentrated.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Prioritize generation, grid and power-access assets over software or capital-light businesses as the durable bottleneck trade.
insights.quote: in 21st century economy, the power is where you really have to be concentrated. That's like the backbone of everything because we've commoditized capital

insights.claim: AI data center regulation is being misread as bearish — regulation favors the incumbent, so owners of existing grid and power access become monopoly toll-takers with balance sheets big enough to absorb compliance costs, just as regulation raised hedge fund startup costs from $500k in the 1990s to roughly $100 million today.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Buy incumbent power and data center operators — including Bitcoin miners pivoting to AI power — into regulatory headlines rather than selling them.
insights.quote: My favorite is Bill Gurley saying regulation favors the incumbent.

insights.claim: Frontier AI labs are running the same incumbent-protection playbook, with Anthropic's strategy characterized as manufacturing safety hysteria to build a regulatory moat that only they can satisfy.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Expect AI safety regulation to entrench the largest labs; it is a barrier-to-entry tailwind for incumbents, not a cost headwind.
insights.quote: has their entire strategy right now is is trying to create a regulatory moat through hysteria

insights.claim: Large-capex physical businesses that cannot be replicated — industrials, machinery and railroads — are the secular long, because AI commoditizes software while margins expand at historical businesses nobody expected, and a deglobalizing two-system world makes hard infrastructure strategically critical.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: The stated thesis of the fund he is joining; positions industrials as a multi-year allocation rather than a cyclical trade.
insights.quote: the secular play here is uh large capex things that you can't uh reproduce and maybe AI commoditizes a lot of things and you get bigger margins from historical businesses you never thought.

insights.claim: Bitcoin's supply overhang came from AI winning the centralization-versus-decentralization battle: treasury companies were taken to the woodshed, and miners pivoting to AI sold coin to fund the transition and are still selling.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Miner and DAT selling explains the drawdown; the trade turns when that forced supply exhausts rather than on any new demand catalyst.

insights.claim: As hash rate falls far enough, mining becomes profitable again, and a scenario where AI infrastructure operators pay more for electricity while the grid gets built out makes Bitcoin mining structurally easier.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Watch hash rate capitulation as the timing signal for a miner and Bitcoin bottom.

insights.claim: The washout of toxic Bitcoin maximalism and the fading dominance of a single figurehead is a tailwind, because an asset whose price action depends on one man's daily decisions carries unacceptable keyman risk.
insights.speaker: co-host
insights.so_what: Reduced keyman concentration lowers the structural risk premium on Bitcoin over time even if it does not help near-term price.
insights.quote: I don't like owning an asset with such keyman risk where all I have to where the price action is entirely determined on like what one guy is deciding on a given day

insights.claim: Crypto is no longer an idiosyncratic problem — it diverged from equities a year ago, equities are the actual problem, and the known fix for equities is printing, which policymakers began preemptively when the S&P was down only two and a half percent.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Crypto's next leg depends on macro liquidity, and the intervention trigger has moved to very shallow equity drawdowns — a bullish liquidity backdrop.
insights.quote: it's no longer a crypto idiosyncratic problem. We we diverge from equities a year ago

insights.claim: With Sailor having raised four billion in cash reserve and BitMine still holding cash, the forced-liquidation blowup risk is off the table, but low volumes, low positioning and the worst seasonal month argue against any high-leverage swing in either direction.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Accumulate slowly rather than sizing up; the clean setup would be a bigger DAT clearing event that has not yet arrived.
insights.quote: the volumes are low, like positioning's low. We're going into the worst seasonal month of the year.

themes.theme: Narrative inceptors and rolling policy-fed bubbles

insights.claim: Crypto's core problem is that it has no narrative an allocator can underwrite — there are many dead projects, and only Bitcoin, stablecoins, Ethereum and yield-generating projects have a defensible case.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Until a new narrative and marketing cycle brings fresh capital, crypto beta stays capped; concentrate in the few assets with a fundable story.
insights.quote: the problem with crypto is it just doesn't have a narrative right now.

insights.claim: Modern market structure runs narrative to capital inflow to retail chasing to high-frequency amplification, and because every inflow causes an asymmetric price move, the last printed price is not information — price is the equilibrium of liquidity.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Size positions against available liquidity rather than headline price; thin-liquidity narratives produce violent, non-fundamental moves in both directions.
insights.quote: That's why like last price is a liar. price is the equilibrium of liquidity.

insights.claim: Every cycle produces 'inceptors' — individuals who find a narrative early and become the figurehead that pulls capital in, such as Gavin Baker for AI, Jack Mallers for the first Bitcoin cycle, Cathie Wood and Josh Wolfe — and the next ones will be a nuclear figurehead like Adam Rodman at Segre Capital and an autonomous-vehicle equivalent.
insights.speaker: Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Tracking who is becoming the narrative figurehead of a sector is a leading indicator of where capital flows next — nuclear and autonomy are the named candidates.
insights.quote: I think there's going to be a nuclear guy. That's my next figure.

insights.claim: You can pre-position for a narrative that does not exist yet precisely because it is not in the price, but the opportunity cost of waiting years for that figurehead to emerge must be weighed against narratives already running elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: A discipline for sizing 'early' positions: pre-narrative bets should be small and time-bounded when live narratives offer better carry.

insights.claim: Price begets narrative begets price — Palantir, Carvana, crypto and semis each took their turn — and as government heavy-handedness increases, these rolling concentrated moves will get more extreme because investors chase whatever the state is visibly supporting, amplified by 3x levered ETFs.
insights.speaker: host and Tyler Neville
insights.so_what: Expect narrower, more violent sector manias in policy-favored areas; rotation timing matters more than broad market direction.
insights.quote: It's not it's not the narrative that kicks things off. It's the

themes.theme: Midterm calendar and the limits of the band-aid regime

insights.claim: This administration has repeatedly played both sides of the manipulation game — tariffs and the Iran conflict were episodes of manufactured volatility — so the current support regime should not be assumed permanent.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate the policy put beyond the political window; the same actors have deliberately created volatility when it suited them.
insights.quote: this administration has also shown a very willing appetite to play both sides of the manipulation game.

insights.claim: The next three months are the peak political incentive window to keep markets afloat: midterms are coming, the House is likely lost, the Senate is a tossup, Trump's approval is at record lows below his first term, and the Iran war and closed strait leave a lot of making up to do.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Assume maximum intervention through the midterms — sell volatility spikes tactically but keep the window explicitly time-limited.
insights.quote: right now we're in the thick of peak political incentive period to keep things afloat. The midterms are coming up. They're probably going to lose the House. The Senate's a tossup.

insights.claim: A post-midterm Democratic sweep would occupy the band-aid machine with daily impeachment hearings and politically popular AI data center moratoriums, creating an air pocket where the constant interventions stop.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: November is the key event risk: hedges for a post-midterm withdrawal of policy support are cheap while everyone focuses on the pre-midterm bid.
insights.quote: the band-aid machine is busy with impeachment hearings and AI data center moratoriums like that does create an air pocket

insights.claim: The band-aid approach requires going back to the well week after week — jawboning the yen, weakening the dollar, intervening again — and since markets are forward-looking, once participants recognize the pattern the suppression may stop working before the midterms arrive.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: The intervention trade decays as it becomes consensus; trading conditions stay choppy and are unlikely to get easier over the next few months.
